Qwen-Image-2.1-Turbo is an […] The post Alibaba Qwen Releases Qwen-Image-2.1-Turbo, an 8-Step 7B Image Model appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Alibaba’s Qwen team has released Qwen-Image-2.1-Turbo , an accelerated checkpoint of its open-weight Qwen-Image-2.1 model. It generates and edits images in 8 denoising steps instead of the base model’s 40-step default . For developers, that means 5x fewer denoising steps on the same 7B architecture, plus a hosted API option. TL;DR Size: 7B parameters in the visual generator, paired with a Qwen3-VL 8B text encoder . Runs on: CUDA GPUs in BF16 via Diffusers. Qwen publishes no Turbo VRAM minimum. Unsloth estimates the base model runs on 11 GB VRAM with GGUF and 24 GB with INT8/FP8 . Performance: Same 2K output and editing feature set as Qwen-Image-2.1, at 8 steps instead of 40. Best: Base Qwen-Image-2.1 scores 60.28 on Qwen-Image-Bench, the top open-weight score Qwen reports. Bottom line (best): 8-step 2K generation and editing in one open checkpoint. Bottom line (worst): Research license only, so commercial self-hosting needs separate permission. What is Qwen-Image-2.1-Turbo? Qwen-Image-2.1-Turbo is an 8-step image generation and editing checkpoint from Alibaba’s Qwen team. It is built on Qwen-Image-2.1 . Turbo keeps the same 7B visual generation architecture. It loads directly with QwenImage21Pipeline in Diffusers. The checkpoint ships with its recommended 8-step sampling schedule saved inside. Generation uses CFG=1 by default. Prefix KV caching reuses the text and reference-image context across denoising steps. How does Qwen-Image-2.1-Turbo work? The underlying architecture is a single-stream DiT with 32 layers and 7B parameters. It uses block-causal attention. Text tokens get a token-level causal mask, while images use a chunk-level bidirectional mask. Text encoder: Qwen3-VL 8B encodes both instructions and condition images. VAE: a 64-channel RGBA autoencoder with 16x spatial compression, which enables native transparency. Scheduler: Flow Matching with Euler discrete scheduling and dynamic shifting. The attention design is what makes prefix caching work. Input images and text are computed once at the first step. Every later step reuses that cache. With only 8 steps, the cached prefix covers most of the conditioning cost. What can it generate and edit? The Turbo model card showcase covers 8 categories. These include portraits, human poses, transparent images, typography and posters, and UI layouts. Editing examples include single-image transformation, multi-reference composition and 4-image interior composition. The base model supports up to 10 reference images and local edits via circles, painted annotations or masks. How do you run Qwen-Image-2.1-Turbo? Setup requires Diffusers from source , along with transformers>=5.17.0 . The checkpoint needs Diffusers PR #14950 , which adds pipeline-configured sampling sigmas. Copy Code Copied Use a different Browser import torch from diffusers import QwenImage21Pipeline pipe = QwenImage21Pipeline.from_pretrained( "Qwen/Qwen-Image-2.1-Turbo", dtype=torch.bfloat16 ).to("cuda") image = pipe( prompt="A ceramic teapot on a wooden table, soft window light", width=2048, height=2048, use_kv_cache=True, ).images[0] For editing, pass image=input_image with an instruction prompt. Supported presets run from 2048×2048 square to 2752×1536 at 16:9. One thing to note here. Setting num_inference_steps alone does not override the saved schedule. Only an explicit sigmas argument does, and Qwen notes other schedules are untested. What does the API cost? Alibaba Cloud Model Studio now hosts both Turbo and Pro. qwen-image-2.1-turbo costs CNY 0.1 per image in most regions, with a 120 RPM limit. qwen-image-2.1-pro costs CNY 0.25 per image, with 20 RPM. Turbo is 2.5x cheaper per image and allows 6x the request rate. A […] The post Microsoft AI Releases Microsoft-Decision-1: A Qwen3.5-9B Decision-Scoring Model appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Microsoft has released Microsoft-Decision-1 , a decision model for routing, classification, verification and agent control. Microsoft-Decision-1 is a decision-scoring model that returns a calibrated probability for each fixed answer option instead of generated text. It is post-trained from Alibaba’s Qwen3.5-9B and available now in Microsoft Foundry and OpenRouter . . TL;DR Size: Built on Qwen3.5-9B; exact parameter count not disclosed. 32,768-token context window. Runs on: Hosted API only (Microsoft Foundry, OpenRouter via Azure). No open weights, no quantized variants, hardware not disclosed. Performance: Highest average accuracy in Microsoft’s 36-benchmark comparison, at 85 ms p50 latency. Best: 83.5% average accuracy across 36 benchmarks, ahead of Quyet-1.0-Large at 81.9%. Worst: Calibration of 92.2, second to Quyet-1.0-Large at 93.1. Text-only, no explanations. Bottom line: Best thing: fast, cheap, calibrated decisions at $0.042 per million input tokens with free output. Worst thing: closed weights, and every benchmark is vendor-run. What is a decision model? A decision model reads an input and scores a closed set of options. It does not write prose. Microsoft frames decision models as a new AI category , built for outputs software can act on immediately. How does Microsoft-Decision-1 work? Microsoft post-trained Qwen3.5-9B for single-pass decision scoring . Given a situation, a question and fixed options, it returns a probability per option in one call. It plans to rebase future versions on MAI and OpenAI models. The Foundry model card lists the supported formats: yes/no, multiple-choice, rating, classification and rubric questions grading of AI responses and proposed agent actions groundedness checks against supplied evidence explicit abstention options such as “cannot tell” Training used public datasets under Microsoft’s Open Data process plus synthetic data. Output is JSON. OpenRouter notes that weights update continually while the API shape stays fixed. How fast and accurate is it? Microsoft compared 9 systems across 36 benchmarks with 147,137 questions . Benchmarks were kept blind from training. Microsoft-Decision-1 led on average accuracy at 83.5%. Its p50 latency was 85 ms, with p95 at 125 ms. That is 4.5 times quicker than Quyet-1.0-Large and 35 times quicker than GPT-6 Sol , which took 3.01 s. Microsoft also tested robustness. It perturbs each request 8 ways, including paraphrasing and option shuffling. The model flipped its decision on 1.3% of perturbations on average. Flips were zero when options were paraphrased, reversed or shuffled. On safety, Microsoft ran 5,250 requests across 11 benchmarks. These covered harmful content, jailbreaks and prompt injection. Microsoft reports correct refusals with high retained utility, without publishing a score. Internal results Microsoft reports Xbox Research: sorted 10,000+ feedback items, 14 times faster and 200 times cheaper than GPT-6 Sol. Copilot quality control: competitive with GPT5.6 Luna and 100 times faster. Microsoft Discovery: 46 times more consistent than LLM scoring, at 3 times the speed. How does it compare with other decision models? Feature Microsoft-Decision-1 Quyet-1.0-Large H2O-Lightning-4B GPT-6 Luna Decisions Developer Microsoft Chinh Nguyen H2O.ai OpenAI Base model Qwen3.5-9B Gemma-4-31B-it (LoRA merged) Qwen3.5-4B Not disclosed Parameters Not disclosed 31.3B 4B Not disclosed Context / input 32,768 tokens 8,000-token prompt (6,000 state) 40,960 (vLLM serve setting) Not disclosed License Proprietary API Apache-2.0 Apache-2.0 Proprietary API Modality Text Text Text and images Text and images Hardware Hosted (Azure) 1x 80 GB GPU, bf16 32 GB GPU tested; 9.1 GB weights Hosted Accuracy (Microsoft, 36 benchmarks) 83.5% 81.9% 77.2% 79.4% Calibration (Microsoft) 92.2 93.1 91.8 89.9 Median latency in Microsoft chart 85 ms 380 ms 210 ms 300 ms Price $0.042/M input, output free Self-host Self-host $0.10/M input, output free Accuracy, calibration and latency rows come from Microsoft’s chart . Competitor latencies there use the JevBench v1.6.1 adjusted median. Is the latency comparison apples to apples? Not fully. Microsoft measured its own model through Foundry. Competitor figures use JevBench’s adjusted median, not raw timings. H2O.ai’s model card disputes this. It states that JevBench’s adjusted figure doubles measured time and adds 0.15 s. H2O says its model’s measured median is 29 ms, not 210 ms. Microsoft-Decision-1 does not appear on the JevBench board. On that board’s official composite, H2O-Lightning-4B ranks #1 at 72.5 . How do developers deploy it? Developers can call it from Microsoft Foundry as a generally available ‘Direct from Azure’ model. On OpenRouter , it runs on the Decisions API, not the chat endpoint. Chat completions SDKs will not work. Pricing is $0.042 per million input tokens, with free output . OpenAI’s Luna decisions endpoint charges $0.10 per million input tokens . What are the limitations? The model card is explicit: Not for text generation, open-ended Q&A, chat, translation or summarization. Text-only. No images, audio or video. No explanations or rationales in the output. Not for sole automated decisions on credit, employment, housing, healthcare or legal rights. Applications must define options, thresholds, escalation paths and human oversight. Key Takeaways Microsoft-Decision-1 scores fixed options with calibrated probabilities, not text. Post-trained from Qwen3.5-9B, with a 32,768-token context window. Leads Microsoft’s 36-benchmark comparison at 83.5% accuracy and 85 ms p50. Costs $0.042 per million input tokens; output tokens are free. Latency comparisons are disputed; independent JevBench results are pending. Check out the official announcement , the Foundry model card and the OpenRouter listing . oldContent: We Work Remotely: Remote jobs in design, programming, marketing and more https://weworkremotely.com/remote-jobs.rss We Work Remotely: Remote jobs in design, programming, marketing and more en-US 60 RETR: Customer Success Manager Anywhere in the World 🇺🇸 United States of America Virginia Sales and Marketing Full-Time <img src="https://we-work-remotely.imgix.net/logos/0171/5755/logo.gif?ixlib=rails-4.0.0&w=50&h=50&dpr=2&fit=fill&auto=compress" /> <p> <strong>Headquarters:</strong> Remote <br /><strong>URL:</strong> <a href="https://retr.app/">https://retr.app/</a> </p> <p class="MsoNormal"><strong><span>About RETR</span></strong></p> <p class="MsoNormal"><span>RETR is a mortgage market intelligence platform. Loan officers use us to find the real estate agents worth building relationships with, mortgage companies use us to recruit top producers, and lenders use us to decide who to lend their money through. More than 55% of the Top 100 mortgage lenders are customers.</span></p> <p class="MsoNormal"><span>We were founded in 2022, we are bootstrapped and profitable, and we have never taken outside money. We grew because loan officers told other loan officers about us. That word of mouth is the whole company in one sentence, and it is why customer outcomes are not a service function here. They are the growth engine.</span></p> <p class="MsoNormal"><span>We are fully remote and we operate on a few principles: </span>lead with value, do the right thing, be generous without keeping score<span>. We hire for honesty, integrity, fairness, accountability, and excellence, and we have very little appetite for process that does not earn its place.</span></p> <p class="MsoNormal"><strong><span>The role</span></strong></p> <p class="MsoNormal"><span>This is one of the first Customer Success Managers at RETR, and you will own a book of our enterprise customers end to end: the relationships, the value they get, the renewal, and the growth.</span></p> <p class="MsoNormal"><span>Our enterprise customers are held today by the founders, sales, support, and enablement, and they are held well. </span>This role exists because the book has outgrown what any of them can carry alongside their own jobs. You get a defined set of accounts and the time to go deep on them: exactly how each one is doing, what it needs next, and where it should be a year from now.</p> <p class="MsoNormal"><span>You will report to our VP of Customer Advocacy and work alongside the account executives who own new business and large expansions, and the trainers who run onboarding and group sessions.</span></p> <p class="MsoNormal"><strong><span>What you own</span></strong></p> <p class="MsoNormal"><span>Four things. Everything else you do should move one of them.</span></p> <p class="MsoNormal"><strong><span>A plan for every customer.</span></strong><span> A short written plan for every account in your book: why they bought, who the people are, what they are trying to accomplish, how they actually use the product, where the risk is, and what happens next. New accounts get one within 30 days. Plans get refreshed before every review and every renewal.</span></p> <p class="MsoNormal"><strong><span>The renewal.</span></strong><span> You own the path to renewal from the day the account joins your book, not from 30 days out. Risk gets named early, in writing, with a plan against it. Nothing should churn without someone having seen it coming.</span></p> <p class="MsoNormal"><strong><span>Expansion.</span></strong><span> Growth comes from value: </span>new use cases, new features, new product lines, new teams and branches, and the seats that follow once people see what it is worth.<span> You run the smaller expansions yourself and bring in an account executive on the larger ones. Part of your pay is tied to this, and it should feel like the natural result of doing the rest of the job well.</span></p> <p class="MsoNormal"><strong><span>Advocates.</span></strong><span> Healthy customers become references, case studies, testimonials, referrals, and beta participants. In an industry this relationship-driven, a customer willing to vouch for us is worth more than most marketing we could buy.</span></p> <p class="MsoNormal"><span>Underneath those four, the work is: knowing how customers use RETR and helping them use it better, building relationships with executive sponsors and daily users alike, reading health from adoption and conversation rather than guessing, and bringing what you hear back into the company so the product and the experience get better.</span></p> <p class="MsoNormal"><strong><span>What this role is not</span></strong></p> <p class="MsoNormal"><span>It is not reactive account management, and it is not a job you win by holding a set number of calls a week. Calls matter, but what matters is what happens on them: the relationship built, the plan moved, the value shown, the joy created.</span></p> <p class="MsoNormal"><span>It is not a support queue. We have a support team and they are good. You are not the escalation path for every ticket in your book.</span></p> <p class="MsoNormal"><span>Because we are still building the Customer Advocacy function, you won't be stepping into a perfectly defined playbook. You'll help create it. We want someone who is energized by that.</span></p> <p class="MsoNormal"><strong><span>How we work</span></strong></p> <p class="MsoNormal"><span>RETR is intentionally lean. Automation before hiring, systems before managers, one to many before one to one. Technology and AI should absorb the work that does not need human judgment, so our people spend their time where people are worth the most: understanding a customer's business, solving a real problem, building a relationship, finding the opportunity nobody else saw.</span></p> <p class="MsoNormal"><span>So we do not want CSMs living in spreadsheets or doing repetitive admin. We want them thinking, and immersed/obsessed with our customers.</span></p> <p class="MsoNormal"><span>We are fully remote and async first. We write things down. We measure what you deliver, and in this role that is the health of your book.</span></p> <p class="MsoNormal"><strong><span>What success looks like</span></strong></p> <p class="MsoNormal"><span>A great CSM here can answer these about any account, at any moment, without opening a file:</span></p> <ul> <li class="MsoNormal"><span>Why did this customer buy RETR?</span></li> <li class="MsoNormal"><span>How are they using it today, and who actually uses it?</span></li> <li class="MsoNormal"><span>Are they getting value, and how do we know?</span></li> <li class="MsoNormal"><span>Who inside the organization cares, and who signs the renewal?</span></li> <li class="MsoNormal"><span>Where could we create more value for them?</span></li> <li class="MsoNormal"><span>What could cost us this renewal?</span></li> <li class="MsoNormal"><span>What happens next, and when?</span></li> &l
